questions.q: A network reaches a training MSE of 0.06 on data whose noise variance is about 0.25, but its test MSE is 0.445. What does this most likely indicate?
options: Underfitting: the network is too small
Overfitting: the network is fitting noise in the training data
A bug in the loss function
That the test set is too easy
questions.explain: Training error far below the noise floor plus a large train/test gap is the signature of overfitting.

questions.q: What does the alpha parameter in scikit-learn's MLPRegressor do?
options: Sets the learning rate
Sets the number of hidden layers
Adds an L2 penalty on the weights
Turns on dropout
questions.explain: alpha is the L2 regularization strength; other libraries call the same idea weight decay.

questions.q: In the lesson, why did early stopping do badly when averaged over five small datasets?
options: Early stopping never works
The 12-point validation set was noisy and could stop training too early
The learning rate was zero
It used the test set for validation
questions.explain: With only 60 rows, 20 percent validation means 12 points, so a noisy dip can trigger stopping before the model has learned.

questions.q: In PyTorch, what happens if you predict with a model containing Dropout but forget to call model.eval()?
options: Nothing; predictions are identical either way
Predictions are randomly noisy because neurons are still being dropped
The model crashes
The weights are reset
questions.explain: In train mode, Dropout keeps switching off random neurons, so repeated predictions differ; eval mode turns dropout off.

questions.q: Besides adding a penalty, which of these is also a form of regularization mentioned in the lesson?
options: Using a smaller network or getting more data
Using a larger network
Training for more epochs with no checks
Removing the validation set
questions.explain: A smaller model has less freedom to memorize; more data makes memorizing harder. An 8-neuron network matched the regularized big one in the lesson.
